♻ ☆ Fast approximation and learning of binary classification tasks in o-minimal structures using ReLU neural networks
Clemens Kinn, Philipp Petersen
We study binary classification tasks whose decision sets are given by definable sets in o-minimal expansions of the real field. Motivated by the cell decomposition theory of definable sets, we introduce traceable sets that isolate the analytical properties of definable sets used for fast approximation by ReLU neural networks. Under uniform bounds on the number of cells and a suitable extension assumption for the boundary functions, we prove that classifiers can be approximated in $L^p$ up to accuracy $\varepsilon>0$ by ReLU neural networks of size $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-p(n-1)/m})$, with depth independent of $\varepsilon$ and polynomially bounded weights. This establishes quantitative approximation rates for suitable definable collections in o-minimal structures using ReLU neural networks. Furthermore, the stated approximation rates are also derived for definable maps under similar geometric assumptions on their smoothness domains. We then obtain statistical learning rates for empirical risk minimization with hinge loss over the approximating ReLU neural network classes. For $N$ uniformly distributed samples, the predicted classifiers achieve expected misclassification error of order $N^{-m/(m+n-1)}$ up to an arbitrarily small polynomial loss.
♻ ☆ Learning pharmacokinetic dynamics with structured neural ODEs for precision dosing
Benjamin Maurel, Agathe Guilloux, Sarah Zohar, Moreno Ursino, Jean-Baptiste Woillard
Individualized dosing requires predicting how a patient's drug exposure would change under a different dose or schedule. However, a model that accurately predicts exposure at the current dose may not reliably predict what happens when treatment changes. We developed two neural models that learn pharmacokinetic dynamics from data without predefined pharmacokinetic equations. The first predicts exposure after a dose change, while the second also allows changes in dosing schedules. In simulations, the second model predicted exposure under new dosing schedules more accurately than competing neural models. On real data of kidney transplant recipients treated with tacrolimus, both models showed lower prediction errors than Bayesian estimation when predicting exposure at a later visit. These findings suggest that incorporating pharmacokinetic principles into neural models can improve predictions needed for individualized dosing.
♻ ☆ Unintended Side Effects of Value Training in LLMs
Siddhesh Pawar, Chen Cecilia Liu, Anna Korhonen, Isabelle Augenstein
As LLMs are increasingly deployed in value-sensitive contexts, aligning them with human values has emerged as a post-training objective in NLP, aimed at instilling additional values and guiding model behaviour. However, current evaluations remain narrow. Because values are interconnected, it is unclear how fine-tuning for specific values alters unrelated capabilities and behaviours. In this work, we adapt four instruction-tuned LLMs across individual Hofstede's value dimensions and evaluate them on both cross-value transfer and broader behaviours. We find that value-specific training produces unintended side effects on untrained values, risk preferences, social cognition, and safety traits. Consequently, we suggest that value alignment after post-training should incorporate broader behavioral evaluations, and we highlight the need to investigate where additional value training might best fit into the pipeline. We release all 48 value-tuned model checkpoints at https://huggingface.co/sidicity/cultural-value-models
comment: 38 pages, 31 figures, 26 tables
♻ ☆ Multimodal Zero-Shot Prediction for Transaction Data at Scale
Parameswaran Kamalaruban, Viktor Drobnyi, Maeve Madigan, Julia Rozanova, David Sutton, Stuart Burrell
Sequential financial transaction data are increasingly being used by financial institutions to train payment foundation models at scale, producing rich contextual embeddings that support applications such as fraud prevention, credit risk assessment, and offer personalization. However, such models are not designed for flexible instruction-following reasoning and require bespoke downstream models for each application. In contrast, large language models (LLMs) provide a natural-language interface for flexible transaction reasoning, yet naively serializing transaction histories into text representations is inefficient and costly. Multimodal fusion architectures bridge these paradigms, injecting transaction embeddings directly into flexible language reasoning pipelines. In this work, we present a systematic study of how transaction embeddings, pretrained at the scale of a global payments network, interact with LLM-based reasoning through embedding injection, transaction-language alignment, and instruction tuning. To do so, we train the Multimodal Instruction Network for Transactions (MINT), which combines a transaction encoder pretrained on billions of real-world payments with multimodal instruction tuning on millions of transaction question-answering examples. We evaluate predictive and extractive question answering, zero-shot generalization to unseen question types, and inference efficiency. Our results reveal a consistent trade-off: compact transaction embeddings improve predictive QA accuracy while substantially reducing input tokens, latency, and memory relative to a text-serialized baseline, whereas serialized histories remain highly competitive for extractive QA. Overall, our empirical findings provide a set of actionable insights and practical guidance for building multimodal transaction-aware language systems at network scale.
comment: An abridged version of this paper was presented at the ICAIF'26 Workshop on Multimodal and Foundation Models in Banking
♻ ☆ A Free Knob: A Sensitivity Audit for Calibration in Threshold-based Evaluation
Md Tanveer Hossain Munim, Bijoy Ahmed Saiem, Al-Amin Sany, Tanzima Hashem
Many benchmarks for rare events score a prediction in three steps: pool the prediction and the target over spatial blocks, threshold each pooled field, and score the resulting contingency table. We show that at a fixed rare threshold the max-pooled Critical Success Index (CSI) cannot separate two different things: how well a system places events, and how well its amplitudes are calibrated. Sharp observations push many blocks above the threshold, while the attenuated predictions of squared-error regression leave those same blocks below it. A monotone calibration map is fitted on held-out data and applied separately to each system. The map needs no retraining and cannot change the order of any two pixels, so whatever part of a difference it reproduces cannot be evidence of better spatial ranking. We report how much of a reported difference the map removes. On SEVIR, two released checkpoints of one architecture differ by -29.5% in extreme-threshold CSI before the control and by +5.3% after it. Across 450 pairwise contrasts among 6 systems, how far apart two systems sit in pooled frequency bias predicts how far their CSI difference moves under the control (r = 0.896 when the map is fitted after pooling), and 64 contrasts reverse sign. At CasCast's published extreme-event operating point, calibration alone removes 88%-106% of the cascade's gain over its backbone across three controls. Calibration also reveals advantages hidden by a better-calibrated baseline. On geostationary infrared imagery, a larger share of the score can be explained by calibration as events get rarer. The problem therefore needs two things at the same time: a threshold that is fixed in advance, and a model whose output is poorly calibrated at that threshold. We recommend reporting pooled frequency bias and a symmetric held-out FreeKnob Audit alongside rare-event pool-and-threshold scores.
comment: Code: https://github.com/munim110/free-knob
♻ ☆ BELLS-O: Evaluating the Operational Trade-offs of LLM Supervision Systems NeurIPS 2026
Leonhard Waibl, Felix Michalak, Hadrien Mariaccia
LLM supervision systems, namely input/output moderation filters and jailbreak detectors, are the primary safeguard against misuse in deployed AI applications, yet existing benchmarks are often vendor-biased, omit cost and latency, and rarely compare specialized guardrails against repurposed generalist LLMs. We present BELLS-O (Benchmark for the Evaluation of LLM Supervision Systems, Operational), an independent operational benchmark that evaluates 33 systems from 17 developers: specialized guardrails (e.g., Llama Guard 4, ShieldGemma-2B, Lakera Guard) and frontier generalists repurposed as supervisors (e.g., GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Grok 4.1 Fast), jointly on detection rate, false-positive rate, latency, and cost. We cover input/output moderation across 11 harm categories, jailbreak detection across 13 attack techniques, and prompt-injection detection, using in-house datasets built from handcrafted prompts, curated external samples, and quality-controlled synthetic generation, with synthetic moderation samples paraphrased to suppress generator fingerprints. Content-moderation runs are repeated five times and all rates reported with 95% intervals. The Pareto frontier reveals use-case-dependent tradeoffs. On content moderation, specialized supervisors are operationally ahead: top systems match the best generalist LLMs on detection (93-96%, no significant difference) at low false-positive rates while running ~5x faster; cost depends more on serving setup than on class. On jailbreak detection, generalist LLMs achieve higher median detection on three of four datasets and lower false-positive rates, but at higher latency and, for closed frontier models, 10-100x higher cost. On prompt injection, the two best dedicated detectors lead. We release the framework, an interactive leaderboard, and four datasets as a vendor-neutral basis for selecting safeguards under deployment constraints.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Track on Evaluations and Datasets). Previously presented at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Trustworthy AI for Good (AI4GOOD). 60 pages, 6 figures; 10-page main text plus appendices
♻ ☆ Semantic-Aware Task Clustering for Constructive and Cooperative Multi-Tasking
Ahmad Halimi Razlighi, Maximilian H. V. Tillmann, Edgar Beck, Bho Matthiesen, Armin Dekorsy
Cooperative multi-task semantic communication (CMT-SemCom) improves task execution performance by leveraging shared representations. However, as we demonstrated in [1], cooperative multi-tasking can be either constructive or destructive, depending on the semantic relationships among tasks. To ensure constructive cooperation, we propose a semantic-aware task clustering method for CMT-SemCom. We have formulated a sequential multi-stage optimization problem in which semantically aligned tasks are clustered once after a short initial training phase, and then end-to-end (E2E) joint training is conducted exclusively within the discovered groups. Specifically, the problem decomposes into two stages: (i) a semantic clustering problem leveraging hierarchical density-based spatial clustering, and (ii) an intra-cluster E2E CMT-SemCom learning problem. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively mitigates destructive cooperation and negative transfer, yielding accuracy gains compared to unclustered multi-tasking and individual training baselines.
comment: Accepted in IEEE GLOBECOM 2026
♻ ☆ Exact Fixed-Point Constraints in Neural-ODEs: Injecting Prior Knowledge into the Network Parameters
Feliciano Giuseppe Pacifico, Duccio Fanelli, Lorenzo Buffoni, Lorenzo Chicchi, Diego Febbe, Raffaele Marino
Neural ordinary differential equations (Neural-ODEs) learn a velocity field from data. Often, however, additional information on the target field is available, such as the location of some of its equilibria or, more generally, its values at given points. We introduce a method to inject this information directly into the parameters of a Neural-ODE, so that a finite set of prescribed fixed points holds exactly throughout training, with no penalty terms and no post-hoc projection. The output matrix is parametrized through the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse, implemented by a thin QR factorization of the hidden features at the prescribed points. This splits the output matrix into a component determined by the constraints and a free one, which shapes the field away from the prescribed points without altering its values there. As a result, the constrained Neural-ODE remains a universal approximator of the continuous vector fields compatible with the constraints. We test the method on a two-dimensional Lotka-Volterra competition model with four equilibria. In vector field regression, the constrained model keeps the fixed-point residual at single-precision round-off, and its test error is up to about five times lower than that of an unconstrained network of the same architecture. A soft penalty on the equilibria lowers the residual only at the cost of accuracy, and still leaves it at least an order of magnitude above that of the constrained model. Trained to convergence on datasets of increasing size, the unconstrained and penalized networks saturate already on small datasets, while the constrained model keeps improving over a wider range. Close to the equilibria and over long time horizons, the constrained model is the most accurate at every dataset size considered. This also holds when the models are trained on observed trajectories, by backpropagation through the ODE solver.
♻ ☆ Mean--Variance Portfolio Selection by Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning: Algorithms, Regret Analysis, and Empirical Study
Yilie Huang, Yanwei Jia, Xun Yu Zhou
We study continuous-time mean--variance portfolio selection in markets where stock prices are diffusion processes driven by observable factors that are also diffusion processes, yet the coefficients of these processes are unknown. Based on the recently developed reinforcement learning (RL) theory for diffusion processes, we present a general data-driven RL approach that learns the pre-committed investment strategy directly without attempting to learn or estimate the market coefficients. For multi-stock Black--Scholes markets without factors, we further devise an algorithm and prove its performance guarantee by deriving a sublinear regret bound in terms of the Sharpe ratio. We then carry out an extensive empirical study implementing this algorithm to compare its performance and trading characteristics, evaluated under a host of common metrics, with a large number of widely employed portfolio allocation strategies on S\&P 500 constituents. The results demonstrate that the proposed continuous-time RL strategy is consistently among the best, especially in a volatile bear market, and decisively outperforms the model-based continuous-time counterparts by significant margins.
comment: 99 pages, includes appendix. Accepted for publication in Management Science
♻ ☆ ART for Diffusion Sampling: A Reinforcement Learning Approach to Timestep Scheduling NeurIPS 2026
Yilie Huang, Wenpin Tang, Xun Yu Zhou
We consider time discretization for score-based diffusion models to generate samples from a learned reverse-time dynamic on a finite grid. Uniform and hand-crafted grids can be suboptimal given a budget on the number of time steps. We introduce Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART), which controls the clock speed of a reparameterized time variable to redistribute computation along the sampling trajectory while preserving the terminal time, with the objective of minimizing the aggregate Euler discretization error. We derive a randomized companion ART-RL that recasts ART as a continuous-time reinforcement learning problem with Gaussian policies, and prove a two-directional bridge between the two: the deterministic ART optimum lifts to an optimal Gaussian policy, and conversely any optimal Gaussian policy must recover the ART control through its mean. This bridge turns continuous-time actor--critic learning into a principled, rather than heuristic, route to the deterministic timestep optimum. Within the official EDM pipeline, ART-RL improves FID on CIFAR--10 across a wide range of budgets; after one-time offline training, the distilled deterministic schedule transfers without retraining to AFHQv2, FFHQ, and ImageNet at no extra inference cost.
comment: 12 pages. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
♻ ☆ Theorem-Proving Agent over Abstract Syntax Tree ICSE
Qiyuan Xu, Joshua Ong Jun Leang, Renxi Wang, Wenda Li, Haonan Li, Luke Ong, Conrad Watt
Interactive theorem proving (ITP) underpins program verification and formalized mathematics, but its manual effort limits scalability. LLM-based proof agents promise to ease this effort, but their heavy token consumption and API cost remain a major obstacle. We trace this cost to a shared root: current agents operate on serialized concrete syntax, emitting proofs as source text and recovering proof states through separate, line-number-based queries, so every edit shifts later lines and forces repeated relocation of errors and states. This same dependence on concrete syntax also blocks adoption of Minilang, a recent proof language that reaches SOTA on LLM-based proving but is too new for LLMs' training corpora. We address both problems by lifting the agent off source text and onto the abstract syntax tree (AST): the model supplies proofs as JSON representations of Minilang's AST -- native to tool-calling LLMs -- and drives the prover through a tree-edit model that fuses proof operations and states into one proof tree, so each operation carries its own subgoal's state, readable directly off the tree. We realize this design in \emph{Agent over AST} (AoA). Against Amazon's Isabelle Agent on miniF2F and NTP4VC-Pearl common success sets, AoA cuts API cost by 2.3--4.7x (normalized input-cache accounting), uses 2.9--6.9x fewer tokens and 3.9--8.9x fewer tool calls, and finishes 1.4--2.0x faster -- while also solving far more problems on the harder verification benchmark.
comment: 13 pages. Accepted at International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE) 2027
♻ ☆ When Can Learned Uncertainty Be Trusted? An Audit of Distributional Reinforcement Learning
Hari Prasad
Many learned predictive models represent their uncertainty as a probability distribution, and planners and policies use this distribution to judge risk. However, the fact that a model outputs a distribution does not tell us whether that distribution captures the uncertainty in the environment which is relevant for a decision. In this work we study this question in distributional reinforcement learning, where the learned return distribution P_θ(Z | s,a) can be compared directly with an environment-grounded distribution P_env(Z | s,a) estimated by snapshot-restart Monte Carlo. Our audit first screens for the claims that a risk-sensitive user would act upon, using the excess Wasserstein gap between the top two actions (which is equal to the mass by which first-order stochastic dominance is violated). Each claim is then tested against ground truth using permutation nulls, bootstrap refutation and FDR control. Across QR-DQN, C51 and IQN on MinAtar (33 runs), 40-95% of the strongest claimed risk trade-offs are refuted at 95% confidence, their placement is statistically indistinguishable from a truth-blind placement, and almost none of them can be confirmed. A similar pattern is seen for a pretrained full-Atari QR-DQN. On positive controls of known magnitude the same audit confirms 96-100% of real claims (correlation 0.89-0.92), so it is able to detect real risk when it is present. Acting on the learned CVaR advice at the most-flagged states gives results ranging from beneficial to significantly worse than chance. Ensembling, risk-sensitive training and recalibration do not fix the problem, and the recalibration experiment indicates that the learned spread has no usable information about the true risk. Based on these results, we suggest that uncertainty estimates, including those of learned world models, should be checked against realized outcomes at the decisions where they are used..
comment: 25 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables (main text); includes supplementary material
♻ ☆ Multi-Task Self-Evolving Harnesses with the Agent as Its Own Optimizer
Qiankai Xu
A harness is the code around a language-model agent that organizes prompts, calls tools, manages context, and controls execution. As models grow stronger, recent work has begun to let agents improve their own harnesses, a line of work known as self-evolving harnesses. In most existing methods, a separate proposer running on a human-designed harness modifies the solver's harness, and a separate harness is evolved for each benchmark. Real-world tasks come from many domains, so both the evolution and the evaluation of a harness should cover a diverse range of tasks. We propose a framework close to recursive self-improvement: the same frozen model, on the same version of the harness, first solves tasks as the solver and then, as the proposer, reads the complete run records and directly edits the harness that runs it. Each evolution batch draws tasks from five benchmarks in different domains. To measure generalization, training and held-out tasks are strictly separated, and we additionally evaluate on five out-of-distribution benchmarks never used during evolution. We frame the evolution process as deep-learning training with two stages, multi-task pretraining and continual training. Starting from a 49-line seed harness, the harnesses evolved by GLM-5.3 and GPT-5.6 Sol gain about 5 points on the in-distribution benchmarks, matching or exceeding Claude Code and Codex, and the GPT-5.6 Sol harness is on par with Codex on five out-of-distribution benchmarks. Continued evolution on Claw-Eval in the second stage then lifts GPT-5.6 Sol and GLM-5.3-Flash above Codex and Claude Code. We also provide an in-depth analysis of the mechanisms that emerged during evolution, including output truncation, history compaction, completion checks, independent review, and visual inspection. Code and the evolved harnesses are available at https://github.com/xqkkk/self-evolving-harness.
♻ ☆ Geometry Matters in Packed 3D Attention NeurIPS 2026
Amil Khan, Anantajit Subrahmanya, B. S. Manjunath
Packing a 3D field into a token sequence gives every token two indices: a coordinate in the sample and a position in memory. Raster, Morton, and block-contiguous layouts change the position and leave the coordinate alone. A positional mechanism indexed by sequence position can therefore learn the memory layout rather than the object, and accuracy on the training layout cannot reveal that it has. We introduce PACK3D, a local-global attention operator that separates memory layout from attention geometry. It attends exactly within a coordinate-defined neighborhood, sees the whole field through pooled summaries, and rotates queries and keys with axial RoPE at token-grid coordinates. Because keys are rotated before pooling, each query-to-summary logit is a weighted sum of query-key terms evaluated at the summarized tokens' displacements from the query. The operator is equivariant to any repacking that carries coordinates, neighborhoods, summary memberships, and within-block slots along with the tokens. When evaluated on Allen WTC-11 microscopy at 262k tokens, PACK3D and a matched packed-sequence RoPE control reach comparable Dice on the training layout. Repacking the same validation volumes then costs the packed control 0.048 macro Dice on average, with a loss in all six seeds, while PACK3D changes by 0.0001. On MSD Heart and Spleen, sequence indexing again changes more predictions under repacking, at little cost in Dice. PACK3D also exceeds a parameter-matched 3D U-Net by 0.009 Dice over six seeds, and a full PACK3D layer runs within 7-31% of window-attention latency while adding a global pathway. Geometry, not storage order, should index attention over packed 3D fields. Code is available at https://github.com/amilworks/Pack3D.
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 (Poster)
♻ ☆ Allocating Recurrent Compute in Looped Language Models
Ruhai Lin, Yiyang Guo, Rui-Jie Zhu, Hao Ye, Jason K. Eshraghian
Looped language models improve reasoning and knowledge manipulation by applying shared computation repeatedly. Existing systems usually repeat an entire layer stack, although a mixer and a dense feed-forward network (FFN) perform different operations and have different costs. We ask a narrower question: what should loop? We view recurrence as repeated composition of a state update and argue that an application is valuable when it exposes a new cross-position influence direction that remains observable at the task readout. Iterative Transport Rank (ITR) describes the cumulative influence trajectory; marginal ITR describes the nonredundant influence contributed by successive applications. This view motivates MixerLoop, which repeats each Gated DeltaNet mixer while applying its dense FFN once. We compare MixerLoop with no recurrence and full-block recurrence at 15M and 110M parameters under the same data, initialization, and architecture. A finite context-off intervention tests whether later mixer applications produce distinct, non-negligible, and beneficial changes at the final language-model readout. MixerLoop surpasses FullLoop on aggregate CORE at 15M and retains 41.5% of its CORE improvement at 110M while reducing recurrent-backbone projection FLOPs by 45.9%. These results show that the benefits of recurrent depth can be retained without repeatedly executing the dense FFN.
♻ ☆ Goodhart in the Planner: Sampling-Based Control Exploits Rewards Learned from Human Preferences
Soovadeep Bakshi, Apurba Bose
Robots increasingly plan by searching against a reward model learned from human preferences; we measure what this search does to the true objective. On HalfCheetah and Hopper with crowd-sourced labels, and on Meta-World drawer-open and plate-slide with synthetic labels and blind labels from the two authors, harder MPPI search cuts true return by up to 76% while held-out label accuracy stays at 0.75-0.97: with human labels the drawer opens in 0 of 20 runs, against 10 of 10 for the cloned policy the planner starts from. The effect persists with a learned dynamics model and with an image scorer. True return roughly follows how far the planner's weights move from its proposals ($\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}}$), and best-of-$N$ action selection with a verifier trained on synthetic labels falls below a single noisy action. We prove that $χ^2$-regularized MPPI at a temperature set by the scorer's error spread on the proposals is worst-case optimal, that no gain can be certified once that spread exceeds the scorer's own, and that an episode's return splits exactly into per-step terms, only some of which the guarantee covers. Calibrated from 100 proposal pairs ranked by true return (an oracle), this rule is the safest fix we test: it keeps on average 86-94% of the cloned policy's return on drawer-open and plate-slide, though it is cautious on window-open, where search helps. Calibrated from a person's own comparisons, it cannot detect a bias the scorer shares with that person; a second person, or correcting for pairs people cannot tell apart, limits the damage.
comment: 21 pages, 4 figures. Equal contribution. Code and results will be released
♻ ☆ BiMuon: A Geometry-Aware Stochastic Bilevel Optimization Approach
Zhen Qin, Zhiyao Zhang, Yingbin Liang, Jia Liu
Stochastic bilevel optimization provides a general framework for many machine learning applications, such as hyperparameter learning, data reweighting, language model alignment, and actor-critic reinforcement learning. However, most existing bilevel optimization methods treat matrix-valued gradients as flattened vectors and perform optimization in the resulting vectorized space, ignoring the matrix structures common in modern neural networks. Moreover, the lower-level (LL) problem curvature can induce significant spectral imbalance in the upper-level (UL) geometry. Such limitations of existing bilevel optimization methods motivate us to develop BiMuon, a geometry-aware stochastic bilevel optimization method that integrates implicit hypergradient estimation in bilevel optimization with Muon-style orthogonalized updates at the UL. To our knowledge, BiMuon is the first stochastic BLO method with Muon-style orthogonalized matrix updates and an $O(ε^{-4})$ iteration-complexity guarantee, matching the best-known rates achieved by Muon-type methods based on matrix parameterizations. To improve computational and parallel efficiency for models with multiple matrix parameters, we further study BiMuon for blockwise diagonal matrix approximation and derive a relative stepsize allocation rule based on UL progress and blockwise LL sensitivity. We evaluate BiMuon on representation learning and blockwise bilevel optimization, providing empirical support for our methods.
♻ ☆ Measure Before You Train: Typed Decision Models vs. a Classical Baseline vs. a Generative LLM for Routing a Personal Multilingual Inbox
Federico Lucca
Personal email agents decide, for every message, its type and urgency and whether to draft a reply, create a task or ignore it. In production these decisions are delegated to a generative LLM or to rules, and their error rate is rarely measured: the stored labels were written by the system itself. We describe Foyer, a self-hosted personal inbox agent, and a measurement protocol (stratified sampling, frozen snapshots, thread-grouped splits, secret redaction, human labels in the review loop) that produces ground truth before any training. On 231 emails in Italian and English we compare eleven systems: the stored production type, a TF-IDF + logistic-regression baseline, local and hosted typed decision models (Tev1, Nimble, Jeva, Jev) and generative LLMs. Four results. The stored production type scores 28% against a 57% majority class. With about two hundred labels a logistic regression has the highest point accuracy on every field (type 0.77 +/- 0.02 over five seeds) at a thousandth of the latency, but on every field at least one hosted model is statistically indistinguishable from it (exact McNemar, Holm-corrected). A generative model recovers part of the sender's relationship to the owner from the text (0.60); inheritance from the contact is right 98.6% of the time where the sender was seen before: it belongs in the contact graph, not in the prompt. Per-email accuracy is not the product metric: composed into actions, the classifier ignores 18% of the emails that needed action, against 4% for the best generative model; a cost-chosen threshold cuts that to 10%, indistinguishable from the hosted decision model's; on the adversarial corpus the thresholded classifier is the cheapest system above a missed-email price of 4. Two blind annotators agree with the reference at kappa 0.81 and 0.86 on type. v4 corrects threshold results computed on a truncated corpus in v1-v3.

♻ ☆ Pro-t-VAE: Closed-Form Student's t Mixtures for Robust Prototype Discovery NeurIPS 2026
Zhikang Xu, Jiarui Xing, Jian Wang
We present a robust deep generative framework for unsupervised image prototype discovery, built on a heavy-tailed Student's t mixture prior, that bridges statistical robustness and mathematical tractability. Existing generative approaches typically rely on noise-prone Gaussian priors or computationally intensive diffusion models; neither simultaneously provides explicit latent structure nor exact analytic optimization. While diffusion models can yield strong priors, iterative sampling and intractable likelihoods limit scalability and interpretability for prototype discovery. We address these issues by constructing a Student's t latent space via a Bayesian scale-mixture formulation. This yields a fully closed-form augmented ELBO for unsupervised Student's t mixture variational autoencoders, which, to our knowledge, is the first such objective applied to robust image prototype discovery, avoiding biased variational approximations and high computational costs in prior heavy-tailed or diffusion-based frameworks. Treating precision as a latent variable automatically modulates each data point's influence, downweighting outliers to learn a data-dependent measure of trust. The result is improved robustness, accuracy, and efficiency, with well-separated latent representations and more stable manifold learning than state-of-the-art methods. We validate our model on standard vision benchmarks and challenging neuroimaging tasks. In brain MRI-driven neurodegenerative disease analysis, our model recovers clean, anatomically coherent prototypes where clinical noise often collapses rare subtypes. These results highlight the ability of our framework to preserve anatomy-associated patterns for precise discovery in clinical settings. Our code is available at: https://github.com/xuzhikangnba/torch-tvae.

♻ ☆ Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II: Unlocking the Memory Potential of Pre-trained File Operations for Long-Horizon Tasks via On-Policy Distillation
Lirui Luo, Kelong Mao, Xinwei Yang, Rongqing Li, Luyu Chen, Kieran Wong, Yudong Guo, Xinrui Wang, Jiayin Zhu, Pu Yao, Gu Simiu, Sulong Xu, Cong Fang
Language-model agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks whose interaction histories exceed the model's active context. They must therefore decide what to write down and what to read back, and when to do either. Recent work has begun to use on-policy distillation (OPD) to make memory control part of the policy, relying on memory tools and compaction protocols that lie outside either model's pre-training. However, this weakens the distillation on both sides: the teacher cannot give useful guidance on an interface it has never used, and the student samples too few meaningful memory actions for that guidance to take effect. To study this problem, we introduce Coding Agent Memory Gym II (CAMG-II), a suite of long-horizon agentic-RL environments spanning Shop, Coding, AutoResearch, General, and Visual. Alongside each environment's native task interface, CAMG-II provides ordinary Bash access and an episode-persistent workspace, enabling the policy to create, revise, search, and reuse files as memory across context replacements. We also introduce Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II (CAMP-II), which trains a single policy jointly across all five environments with fully asynchronous OPD to learn this file-based memory behavior directly from a frozen teacher with a prior for file operations. On CAMG-II, CAMP-II obtains 2.97 times the gain of the strongest OPD baseline. The memory behavior CAMP-II learns generalizes to two external benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, with improved success rates.

♻ ☆ SkillDuet: Co-Evolving Models and Skills through Response Feedback
Xingguang Ji, Ziqiang Dong, Yubo Zhang, Xi Leng, Ninghua Yan, Yang Yang, Guanjun Jiang
During reinforcement learning, experience can be both internalized in LLM parameters and retained externally as reusable textual skills. Parameter updates alter the model's behavior and the interaction experience from which new skills are extracted. These skills, in turn, guide the model's subsequent interactions and parameter updates. As the model's capabilities evolve, previously beneficial skills may become redundant or detrimental. We present SkillDuet, a framework that coordinates parameter updates and skill evolution through model response feedback. Skills extracted from on-policy trajectories guide parameter updates through OPD at every step. A response-based score, Strength, ranks candidate skills by the magnitude of the shift they induce in the current model's responses, and the highest-scoring skills are periodically consolidated into a persistent global skill set (Global). The updated model and Global jointly guide subsequent interactions, generating experience for further parameter and skill updates. With Qwen3-4B, SkillDuet achieves success rates of 98.57% on ALFWorld and 92.97% on WebShop, exceeding the matched SEED-API baseline by 2.86 and 5.47 percentage points, respectively. Ablations show that response-based skill selection and Global consolidation improve task performance. Further experiments show that the benefits of retained skills depend on both their content and their compatibility with the model. SkillDuet provides a concrete mechanism for model-skill co-evolution and skill-level recursive self-improvement.

♻ ☆ Automata from Agent Traces: Failure and Next-Step Prediction NeurIPS 2026
Seonglae Cho, Franklin Cardenoso Fernandez, Umar Mohammed, Zekun Wu, Kleyton Da Costa, Ilham Wicaksono, Adriano Koshiyama
LLM-based agents execute multi-step tasks, but their behavioral structure remains opaque: long unstructured traces resist the safety auditing and runtime monitoring that deployment requires. Existing approaches operate per-trace or success-only, so they miss the cross-run topology that links next-step and failure prediction. To recover that shared structure, we collapse an entire trace corpus into a single, compact finite-state machine (FSM) that serves as a structural substrate for the otherwise unpredictable behavior of LLM agents. Across twelve public datasets, the FSMs are compact (7-43 states), replay held-out data at >=0.997 fitness with near-identical topology across splits, and build in milliseconds. This substrate addresses both prediction goals. For next-step prediction, FSM-state context outperforms Agent Workflow Memory on every ground-truth-matched dataset. For failure prediction, per-state behavioral features reach held-out AUROC up to 0.94, and an online monitor ranks failing runs above passing ones from a partial trace, triggering early stopping well before completion. Behavioral topology thus appears shaped more by the deployment harness than by the LLM, providing a model-agnostic structural primitive for safety auditing and runtime monitoring.

♻ ☆ Control Reinforcement Learning: Interpretable Token-Level Steering of LLMs via Sparse Autoencoder Features NeurIPS 2026
Seonglae Cho, Zekun Wu, Adriano Koshiyama
Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model activations into interpretable features, but existing methods reveal only which features activate, not which change model outputs when amplified. We introduce Control Reinforcement Learning (CRL), which trains a policy to select SAE features for steering at each token, producing interpretable intervention logs: the learned policy identifies features that change model outputs when amplified. Adaptive Feature Masking encourages diverse feature discovery while preserving singlefeature interpretability. The framework yields new analysis capabilities: branch point tracking locates tokens where feature choice determines output correctness; critic trajectory analysis separates policy limitations from value estimation errors; layer-wise comparison reveals syntactic features in early layers and semantic features in later layers. On Gemma 2 2B across MMLU, BBQ, GSM8K, HarmBench, and XSTest, CRL achieves improvements while providing per-token intervention logs. These results establish learned feature steering as a mechanistic interpretability tool that complements static feature analysis with dynamic intervention probes

♻ ☆ TIDE: Token-Level Credit Assignment via Entropy-Gated Bounded Deviation
Qiaoman Zhang, Shunhua Min, Xiang He, Zhenghan Zhang, Yuting Zhang, Guangxian Li, Yunzhu Kuang, Rui Jiang, Jingyan Zhang, Chaoyue Li, Jiayu Ding
Reinforcement learning (RL) is central for aligning large language models (LLMs) with complex reasoning, yet the leading critic-free algorithm, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), broadcasts a single sequence-level advantage uniformly across long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) generations and constrains exploration with an unbounded Kullback-Leibler (KL) penalty, which dilutes token-level supervision and induces gradient instability and mode-seeking conservatism. We propose TIDE (Token-level Importance via Deviation and Entropy), a critic-free RL framework that reinterprets distribution deviation as a guiding signal rather than a rigid penalty. TIDE replaces the volatile reverse KL divergence with the bounded Hellinger distance, safely quantifying token-level exploration without risk of gradient explosion. To separate genuine reasoning breakthroughs from confident hallucinations, an entropy gating mechanism scales this deviation by the policy's predictive uncertainty, and the gated scores redistribute the sequence-level advantage across tokens. The resulting updates amplify exploratory steps while suppressing low-entropy deviations, without a value network and with negligible overhead. Across in-domain, held-out, and out-of-domain benchmarks, TIDE outperforms strong critic-free baselines: on the Qwen2.5-32B backbone it reaches 60.0% and 46.0% Avg@32 accuracy on AIME 2024 and AIME 2025, respectively, above competitive baselines such as DAPO. Token-level attribution, causal perturbation, and exploration analyses further support the interpretation that the entropy-gated deviation identifies pivotal reasoning steps rather than merely perturbing optimization dynamics.
♻ ☆ Label-Wording Augmentation in a Typed-Decision Encoder: Gains on Unfamiliar Words, Not on Abbreviations or Codes
Vladimir Beskorovainyi
Typed-decision models score options that the caller supplies at request time, so their accuracy depends on label wording that the model's developer does not control. We compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder, Ru-Jev, trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks; the later release adds an augmentation that presents labels in several surface forms. Holding questions fixed and varying only how eighteen routing labels are worded, we evaluate ten label vocabularies at five and eighteen candidates, checked for overlap with the training data. On held-out vocabularies made of ordinary or borrowed words (jargon, office slang, department names), the augmented release has higher point accuracy in all fourteen cells, by up to 0.24. Several of these gains rest partly on one label that the earlier release almost never chose; fitting one bias per option removes part of them, while the jargon gain largely survives. On abbreviations and opaque codes the augmented release gives no usable gain: its loss on 17 abbreviations unrelated to training (-0.060) is one label and disappears after the same correction. The comparison is between two trained releases, not a controlled ablation, and the earlier recipe varies across seeds by up to 0.098 on the strictest slice. On two datasets neither release saw, accuracy moves by -8.4 and +5.6 points, narrowed to -3.4 and +1.4 by the per-option biases; on a third, scientific rubrics, the augmented release is ahead of both runs of the earlier recipe after the correction. Rankings of ten training checkpoints disagree across the three unseen datasets, so none of them should choose the checkpoint. We also report four evaluation hazards from comparing the two releases.

♻ ☆ Square-Root Regret for Adversarial Multiplayer Bandits without Collision Information or Shared Randomness
Chenyu Gan
We study cooperative multiplayer bandits with adversarial rewards and no collision information. In each of $T$ rounds, each of $m$ labeled players picks one of $K>m$ arms. A player alone on its arm receives that arm's reward in $[0,1]$; players who share an arm receive $0$. Each player observes only its own reward, so it cannot distinguish a collision from an arm with zero reward, and there is neither shared randomness nor a communication channel. Bubeck, Li, Peres and Sellke (2020) obtained regret $\widetilde O(KT^{3/4})$ for two players and $\widetilde O(mK^{3/2}T^{1-1/(2m)})$ for $m$ players, and conjectured that regret $Ω(T^{2/3})$ is unavoidable already for two players. We refute this conjecture. We give a strategy whose expected regret against every oblivious adversary is $O(m^{3/2}\sqrt{KT}\log^2(KmT))$, which is optimal in $K$ and $T$ up to logarithmic factors. Three ideas make this possible. (i) Bits are sent through deliberate collisions as random parity checks, and the regret spent while a message is delayed is charged to the number of arms with positive reward rather than to elapsed time: an adversary that jams the channel with zero rewards forfeits the regret it could inflict. (ii) An exponential-weights learner over sets of arms combines a frequently resampled coordinator arm with a follower assignment that changes only $O(\sqrt{mT/K})$ times in expectation; delayed updates are reconstructed exactly. (iii) We teach the followers a privately chosen row index in a fixed public table using reward observations alone, allowing them to coordinate without shared randomness. The bound holds simultaneously for all reward matrices, even ones chosen with knowledge of the table, and a random table works with probability $1-O(1/(KmT))$.

♻ ☆ Corrected Integrated Laplace Approximation for Bayesian Inference in Latent Gaussian Models NeurIPS 2026
Jinlin Lai, Charles C. Margossian, Daniel Sheldon
Latent Gaussian models (LGMs) are a popular class of Bayesian hierarchical models that include Gaussian processes, as well as certain spatial models and mixed-effect models. Efficient Bayesian inference of LGMs often requires marginalizing out the latent variables. For LGMs with a non-Gaussian likelihood, exact marginalization is not possible and a popular approach is to do approximate marginalization with an integrated Laplace approximation (ILA). Using ILA produces an approximate posterior which, in some settings, can differ significantly from the correct posterior, which impacts downstream applications. We propose an importance sampling scheme to correct the error introduced by ILA. By increasing the number of samples in importance sampling, the posterior with ILA converges to the correct posterior. This idea is realized with various techniques, including pseudo-marginalization, quasi-Monte Carlo and randomized quasi-Monte Carlo. We implement our methods in an automatic differentiation framework to support gradient-based algorithms when doing inference on the hyperparameters. For the latter, we specifically consider the use of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. We demonstrate the benefits of reduced error in various applied models.

♻ ☆ The Decomposition Is the Fingerprint: Per-Component Identity for Agent Skills
Hongliang Liu, Yuhao Wu, Tung-Ling Li
AI agents increasingly acquire and execute skills at runtime: bundles of prompt instructions, executable code, and tool declarations fetched from marketplaces and other agents. Governing them needs a stable notion of skill identity, yet cryptographic hashing is engineered to destroy the very similarity we need, as a one-character edit scrambles the digest. We present a compact, locality-sensitive fingerprint that embeds each component of a skill and projects it to bits with a multi-bank SimHash, giving a fixed 120-byte signature compared in constant time by Hamming distance. Our central claim is that keeping the fingerprint as a per-component triple (prompt, code, tools), rather than a single score, is what makes it useful: the triple recovers skill-family identity through paraphrase, renaming, refactoring, and controlled code translation when another component remains shared, while independent multilingual reimplementation is not recovered; it also localizes which component carries the reuse. We claim lineage, not behavioral equivalence: identity supplies the structural axis of a registry and leaves safety to behavioral verification. The fingerprint reaches an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.974 (95% CI [0.956, 0.994]) over 4,950 pairwise comparisons while using 77x fewer bits than the embedding it approximates, with ranking preserved in expectation and finite-bit concentration; the per-component split turns one number into relationship classification, families, novelty, and a portable "SkillBOM" for a skill registry. On a 906-skill injection benchmark the fingerprint recognizes injected skills as tampered copies of a known base and localizes the change, but recognition is not trust: it remains, by design, an identity signal complementary to behavioral verification rather than a safety verdict.
♻ ☆ Versatile yet Efficient Network Traffic Analysis: Offloading Network Foundation Model to SmartNIC NDSS 2027
Chungang Lin, Xuying Meng, Tianyu Zuo, Weiyao Zhang, Meng Shen, Ruijie Zhao, Guanming Che, Ruiqi Meng, Ziyue Huang, Haitong Luo, Zhiwei Xu, Yujun Zhang
Pervasive encryption makes large-scale labeling infeasible for traffic analysis, while security operations demand edge analysis to avert service degradation and vulnerabilities. These pressures have produced two research lines that advance 1) versatile analysis, via network foundation models for low label dependency, and 2) efficient analysis, via hardware offloading for low analysis latency. However, co-achieving versatility and efficiency via such lines has appeared incompatible, with prior work advancing one while compromising the other, yet we show that this incompatibility is a consequence of polarized design choices across the three components of traffic analysis systems, i.e., traffic processing, model architecture, and analysis execution. In response, we present Nepco, a versatile yet efficient network traffic analysis system that offloads network foundation models to SmartNIC. Our key observation is that discriminative traffic information often exhibits localized patterns within byte sequences, motivating versatile yet efficient localized byte-sequence modeling. To exploit this without incurring the latency bottlenecks of complex encoding steps, we employ a hardware-friendly processing strategy that directly embeds raw byte sequences. To maintain versatility across diverse tasks characterized by spatially shifting features, we explore an observation-driven convolution architecture equipped with hardware-friendly scoring and gating designs. By exploiting translation invariance, this design dynamically locates and extracts salient semantic signatures irrespective of their byte-level offsets. We prototype Nepco on the NVIDIA BlueField-3 SmartNIC with multi-engine collaborative analysis execution. The experimental results demonstrate that Nepco achieves macro F1 competitive with the best performances achieved by 8 state-of-the-art network foundation models...

♻ ☆ MAC: A Conversion Rate Prediction Benchmark Featuring Labels Under Multiple Attribution Mechanisms KDD 2026
Jinqi Wu, Sishuo Chen, Zhangming Chan, Yong Bai, Lei Zhang, Sheng Chen, Chenghuan Hou, Xiang-Rong Sheng, Han Zhu, Jian Xu, Bo Zheng, Chaoyou Fu
Multi-attribution learning (MAL), which enhances model performance by learning from conversion labels yielded by multiple attribution mechanisms, has emerged as a promising learning paradigm for conversion rate (CVR) prediction. However, the conversion labels in public CVR datasets are generated by a single attribution mechanism, hindering the development of MAL approaches. To address this data gap, we establish the Multi-Attribution Benchmark (MAC), the first public CVR dataset featuring labels from multiple attribution mechanisms. Besides, to promote reproducible research on MAL, we develop PyMAL, an open-source library covering a wide array of baseline methods. We conduct comprehensive experimental analyses on MAC and reveal three key insights: (1) MAL brings consistent performance gains across different attribution settings, especially for users featuring long conversion paths. (2) The performance growth scales up with objective complexity in most settings; however, when predicting first-click conversion targets, simply adding auxiliary objectives is counterproductive, underscoring the necessity of careful selection of auxiliary objectives. (3) Two architectural design principles are paramount: first, to fully learn the multi-attribution knowledge, and second, to fully leverage this knowledge to serve the main task. Motivated by these findings, we propose Mixture of Asymmetric Experts (MoAE), an effective MAL approach incorporating multi-attribution knowledge learning and main task-centric knowledge utilization. Experiments on MAC show that MoAE substantially surpasses the existing state-of-the-art MAL method. We believe that our benchmark and insights will foster future research in the MAL field. Our MAC benchmark and the PyMAL algorithm library are publicly available at https://github.com/alimama-tech/PyMAL.

♻ ☆ Rethinking Floorplan Generation with Space Syntax: From Design Theory to Model Improvement
Zhuoyang Jiang, Dongqing Zhang, Qingxiang Liu, Yuxuan Liang
Architectural design increasingly adopts generative AI (GenAI) for floorplan generation, an early-stage design task exploring how spaces should be organized for use. Yet fidelity objectives inherited from native visual and geometric generators do not automatically capture this design purpose. This organization remains largely implicit in generated representations, limiting direct evaluation and feedback. Drawing on space syntax, an established architectural design theory, the Space Syntax Integration Operator (SSIO) recovers convex-space access graphs across heterogeneous formats. This theory-grounded shared intermediate representation, which we call a design container, supports evaluation and model understanding of spatial design. Applying SSIO to four residential corpora spanning 15 countries reveals public spaces' integration levels are highest, with corpus-dependent distributions. These patterns underpin the RPLAN-SSI benchmark, an empirical design reference system assessing population-level functional-profile alignment (IPD) and distributional alignment of within-plan public-space advantage (PIAD). Comparison with this residential reference reveals a design gap: public spaces in generated floorplans have a smaller integration advantage over other spaces. To address this gap, Space Syntax-Guided Post-Training (SSPT) provides a plug-and-play design-learning interface: SSIO-derived RL feedback reduces IPD and PIAD across five heterogeneous diffusion backbones while preserving native mechanisms. We further discuss how this approach may inform GenAI applications in other design domains.

☆ AgentSSL: Can MLE Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data? NeurIPS 2026
Ethan Lin, Akanksha Sarkar, Ziang Liu, Kristin Branson, Jennifer J. Sun
Applying machine learning systems to new domains introduces bottlenecks in both labeled data acquisition and manual pipeline engineering. While recent MLE agents show promise in automating pipeline design, they have been studied almost exclusively in fully supervised settings, leaving them untested in realistic regimes where labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant. In this work, we introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning (AgentSSL), framing SSL as a program search problem and studying how agents navigate this space under limited supervision. We find that even under weak feedback and matched compute, agents can synthesize code that combines and adapts established SSL techniques, exceeding the strongest human-engineered baselines in 8 of 12 settings by up to +21.8%. However, our results identify program selection as a critical bottleneck in AgentSSL, where performance drops by as much as 47% when selecting based on the agent's feedback metric. To systematically study this bottleneck, we introduce ProgramSelectBench, a large-scale benchmark with a combined total of 16,977 agent-generated and human-engineered SSL programs, and evaluate both unsupervised and active program selection methods. We further evaluate AgentSSL on real-world ecology detection tasks, highlighting the opportunities and challenges of transferring agent-discovered strategies beyond controlled benchmarks.

☆ CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation
Peiwen Li, Harshit Verma, Sophia Zhou, Haiwen Wang, Ngoc Bui, Heng Chang, Fei Fei, David van Dijk, Rex Ying
Coding agents tackle successive tasks on an evolving repository, carrying forward edits and writing memory before the next task is known. Selecting memory for unknown next tasks requires balancing future usefulness against the costs of writing and reading it. The actor must also decide when acting on available memory saves effort as the task unfolds. We introduce Coding-Repository Memory (CoReMem), a cost-internalizing framework that guides memory design and actor adaptation through measured memory value on the next task. Prospective segment valuation compares runs of the next task with and without individual trajectory segments from the same inherited repository state, guiding a compact memory built around anchors: repository locations and executable checks. Actor adaptation estimates on-policy memory value within rollout groups with and without memory, using a reward that prioritizes resolution and penalizes step count in successful runs. Provenance-gated value credit assigns the additional value term to steps identified as using memory-supplied anchors, while every step retains outcome credit. On ChainSWE, CoReMem raises the 27B actor's resolve rate from 21.0% to 25.7%, with 17% fewer steps and 11% fewer total cache-aware tokens, including memory-module calls, relative to the untrained actor model without memory.
☆ Sketching Language Models for Context Attribution
Christopher Liaw, Aranyak Mehta, Grigoris Velegkas, Felix Zhou
Context attribution asks how removing parts of a prompt changes a language model's output. We study leave-one-out (LOO) attribution for a prompt of $n$ tokens and a fixed measurement function. Computing all LOO values directly requires $n$ model evaluations. Under a stability assumption, our algorithm estimates all LOO values to error proportional to $\varepsilon$ with constant probability using $O(\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}/\varepsilon)$ evaluation calls. To complement our upper bound, we prove a matching $Ω(\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}/\varepsilon)$ lower bound on the number of evaluation calls in an oracle model. Empirically, we verify coefficient decay consistent with stability and evaluate the performance of our sketching algorithm on a small language-model retrieval task. Technically, our result is based on a sketching algorithm for arithmetic circuits whose Taylor coefficients satisfy the stability condition recently introduced by Gunn [Gun26]. A direct adaptation of their forward differentiation sketches would require $\widetilde{O}(\log(n)/\varepsilon^2)$ evaluation calls. Our key observation is that we can apply forward differentiation to the backpropagation circuit, with only constant overhead over a forward sketch of the same Taylor degree. This reduces the variance of the sketches and is key to our improved evaluation bound. Our lower bound builds on the techniques of Amsel, Chen, Duman Keles, Halikias, Musco, and Musco [ACDH+26, SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications] for lower bounding the number of matrix-vector queries to estimate the diagonal elements of random matrices.
☆ Classical Energies Learn to Reason 1,000x Faster than Looped Models
Benjamin Hoover, Hugh Blayney, James C. R. Whittington
Looped models have emerged as a prominent paradigm for reasoning, with successes on simple reasoning puzzles such as Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique. However, these models can be unstable, slow to train, and use many parameters and FLOPs to solve simple puzzles. Descent on an energy not only mitigates these issues but also offers advantages: built-in early stopping, compute that adapts to problem difficulty, fast training without differentiating through a solver, and interpretable weights that learn the constraints of the puzzle. Here we demonstrate this with a learned version of Hopfield & Tank's energy from the 80s, which we term CRAM, solves 99.996% of Sudoku-Extreme and 100% of Maze-Unique test puzzles after 42 ms and 132 ms of training on one GPU, at least 1,000x faster than looped models on these tasks. CRAM also matches baseline looped models at their highest accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme using at least 282x fewer inference FLOPs. Our work suggests two things. First, that energies are an extremely promising direction for training reasoning from data. Second, a caution against using trivially solvable benchmarks like Sudoku and Maze to test the scalability of looped reasoning techniques.
☆ Consistent Video-to-Video Translation via Explicit Correspondences ECCV 2026
Gaurav Parmar, Zhengqi Li, Richard Zhang, Jun-Yan Zhu, Srinivasa Narasimhan, Eli Shechtman, Yotam Nitzan
Interactive video-to-video applications require real-time generation while maintaining long-range temporal consistency. However, recent methods achieve speed by restricting attention to a fixed-length causal window. This limits long-range consistency whenever relevant history falls outside the context window. To address this limitation, we introduce vid2vid-long, a correspondence-based approach grounded in a simple observation. Video-to-video translation provides an explicit cross-frame reference: the regions that match in the input video should match in the output video too. Concretely, we compute patch-level correspondences in the input, guiding retrieval of previously generated outputs in the corresponding regions, and condition the model on these patches through correspondence cross-attention. Our experiments demonstrate that vid2vid-long consistently improves long-range temporal consistency across recent video models while preserving generation quality and real-time performance.

☆ Goal Encoding in LLMs
Arnab Sen Sharma, Eric Todd, Sheridan Feucht, Andy Arditi, Rohit Gandikota, Natalie Shapira, Gabriele Sarti, Constanza Fierro, Lisa Schut, David Bau
We investigate whether and how LLMs encode goals: internal neural representations that precede and guide action, and that are flexible enough to be realized through many different execution paths. We construct a coding setting with multiple sub-tasks that allows us to evaluate goal-seeking behavior and the selection of sub-goals. In this setting, we localize an encoding of the next sub-goal in the outputs of a sparse set of attention heads. The same heads can be used to decode the LM's future actions in natural language (e.g., "I'm checking if a word is a palindrome"). We verify that this encoding is causal for next action and is plastic: transplanting it into a different environment, e.g., another programming language, triggers the same operation realized with a different sequence of tokens. The LM also sustains the encoding throughout the action's execution, which is puzzling because a transformer LM without recurrence cannot carry a state forward for more tokens than it has layers left. We propose that it does not need to. Under a non-recurrent goal-seeking (NRGS) account, the LM frequently re-reads the goal from the task specification, compares it with the progress visible in the growing context, and pursues what remains. We test the predictions of this account with targeted causal interventions.

☆ Metal Sandbox: Isolated Execution and Command Scheduling for GPU Coding Agents on Apple Silicon

On-device inference requires kernels that make effective use of local accelerators. Efficient training and evaluation of models that generate Apple Metal kernels benefit from native macOS tools and concurrent agent sessions. These sessions alternate between model requests, development commands, and GPU execution, leaving GPU capacity idle for much of a rollout. We present Metal Sandbox, infrastructure that combines restricted per-instance file access, native command execution, and command-level scheduling across interconnected Macs. Each agent retains its workspace and private development environment. Parallel commands can run concurrently, while serial commands share one execution slot per node; eligible waiting commands can migrate to available Macs and return results to the original agent. Integration with Harbor supports task execution, automatic verification, and rollout collection through a common workflow. Controlled experiments on four Mac mini M4 nodes achieve $1.68\times$--$2.05\times$ gains in command throughput under concentrated demand. Sixteen static agent traces give an estimated $2.14\times$ sustained-throughput gain for four sessions per node versus one, assuming continuously replenished sessions and unchanged mean durations. Replaying these measured traces under dynamic scheduling reduces mean tool waiting by 18.8% and batch elapsed time by 22.3%, assuming unchanged phase durations. Metal Sandbox and its Harbor integration are open-source on GitHub.

☆ Synthesis Smuggling: Maliciously Hiding Inferred Personal Attributes in LLM Outputs

We propose Synthesis Smuggling, a novel threat model in which an adversarial LLM infers sensitive information about a user from routine assistance-seeking interactions and steganographically encodes that into innocuous-looking model-generated content. The user may then unknowingly transmit that information by sharing the generated artifact, say as an email, social-media post, or message, through ordinary communication channels. An adversary monitoring these channels can discover this information. We demonstrate this threat by training two open-weight models to infer gender and age-group labels from conversational cues and encode their predictions using invisible characters or word choices. These results show that user-shared model outputs can become a covert channel for personal inferences, even when the model itself has no direct means of contacting an adversary.
☆ LiveGeo: Benchmarking Geographic Agents in Continuously Evolving Worlds
Pengcheng Zhou, Xuanyu Liu, Yanchen Yin, Tianjie Ju, Bobo Li, Shengqiong Wu, Hao Fei, Mong-Li Lee, Wynne Hsu
We introduce GeoWorld, a controllable and continuously evolving geographic environment platform for LLM agents, and LiveGeo, a benchmark for evaluating reliable decision-making in real-world geographic environments using GeoWorld. Unlike existing evaluations that largely reason and plan over fixed geographic states, GeoWorld is grounded in real-world geographic structure and allows external world states to evolve along their own temporal processes while preserving verifiable state histories. LiveGeo places geographic tasks within this evolving environment, requiring agents to actively acquire task-relevant information, verify whether the evidence supporting prior decisions remains valid, and revise their plans when necessary. Our results reveal that even frontier LLMs struggle with static tasks, with no model consistently excelling across tasks, while strong static performance does not ensure dynamic reliability. Further analysis identifies a key bottleneck: agents struggle to acquire and translate relevant evidence into valid decisions and maintain their correctness as the world evolves. By releasing LiveGeo together with its GeoWorld platform, we aim to provide the community with a flexible and extensible infrastructure for studying the next generation of agents capable of reliable action in evolving geographic worlds.

Samidha Verma, Ankit Anand, Sayan Ranu
Modern automated heuristic discovery (AHD) systems increasingly rival hand-crafted heuristics by leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to iteratively mutate and refine solutions. A natural assumption is that more powerful and more expensive models consistently yield better heuristics. We challenge this empirically: across multiple NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems, we find no consistent advantage for larger, costlier models. This raises a deeper question: given a pool of LLMs spanning frontier and freely hosted or open-weight models, how should one adaptively select which model to invoke at each step of the search? The challenge is non-trivial. The optimal LLM may shift over the course of a run, and because one LLM's output seeds the context for subsequent calls, each model's reward signal is non-stationary and entangled across the heuristic population, thus violating the independence assumptions of classical online decision-making settings. We address this through Ballad (Bandit-based LLM Routing for Automated Heuristic Discovery), an online bandit algorithm that learns to orchestrate a pool of LLMs into an ensemble that matches or exceeds what any soloist LLM achieves alone. This orchestration is powered by an LLM selection policy that favors rare, high-scoring heuristics over stable averages, a DAG-based credit propagation mechanism through the genealogy of the heuristic population, and discounting of stale observations to remain attuned to each model's current utility. Across five NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems and a pool of four models of varying capability and cost, Ballad not only matches the best individual LLM in hindsight but, in several cases, surpasses every individual model while reducing API cost by up to 65.6% relative to always using the strongest model.

In interactive systems where users engage with LLMs, users are adaptive and, after observing LLM responses, can change their prompting strategy, as well as the type and difficulty of subsequent tasks. Thus model responses can influence the set of prompts on which the model is subsequently evaluated. We study the implications of this user adaptivity and prompt endogeneity for the evaluation of LLMs. We define two classes of estimands for comparing models: the common-distribution effect, which compares model performance on the same distribution of prompts, and the induced-distribution effect, which compares each model on the prompt distribution generated through user interaction. We show that offline benchmark evaluation and live A/B testing target different quantities, with the standard difference-in-means estimators for the two methods converging to the common-distribution effect and the induced-distribution effect, respectively. This distinction can affect decision-making: the two comparisons can rank models differently and lead to discrepancies in deployment recommendations. We characterize when such ranking reversals occur and provide a sufficient condition under which the rankings are guaranteed to agree. This result provides a practical heuristic for assessing whether offline evaluation is sufficient to reproduce the decision suggested by a live experiment. Third, we show, in a stylized linear model of interactions, that user adaptivity can increase variance in estimation. Finally, we discuss implications of user adaptivity for the interpretation of experiments and show that adaptivity creates a common mechanism leading to common evaluation challenges, such as reward hacking and novelty effects. Together, this work highlights the necessity of measuring both model performance as well as changes in the user behavior that the model induces.

This paper presents Al Ghasali, a computational framework designed to formalize and simulate Islamic jurisprudential (Fiqh) rulings. Building upon recent set theoretic formalizations of al sabr wa al Taqsim that extract minimal operational rules as simple Horn clause logical programs, this work proves that the semantics of closed Fiqh chapters collapse completely to deterministic Finite State Automata (FSA). We establish a formal computational hierarchy, demonstrating that restricting formalization to finite propositional Horn theories guarantees decidability and constant time (O(1)) verdict extraction after offline compilation. The framework formally proves that hierarchical compositions of sub-chapter FSAs preserve this O(1) complexity, and that temporal juristic requirements, such as Tartib (order), are deterministically flattened into static ontological states, preserving the memoryless property of the automaton. To generate human-readable juristic summaries, Al Ghasali incorporates Large Language Models (LLMs) via an architecture where the deterministic FSA strictly controls the probabilistic LLM. Crucially, the paper formulates sufficient design safety conditions for this FSA LLM integration, ensuring strict adherence to the epistemological boundaries of Usul al Fiqh. To neutralize the risk of LLM hallucination, the system employs a Grammar Guided Constrained Decoding mechanism. We formally define the mapping function that dynamically constructs unambiguous right linear grammars from the FSA execution history. The paper mathematically proves that this architecture, augmented by a Bounded Neutral Lexicon and Valence Locking, guarantees the absolute absence of Decisional Hallucination, Juristic Factual Hallucination, and Semantic Inversion reducing the LLM to a pure linguistic transformer of deterministic juristic facts

☆ Scalable Conversational Assessment: Chat-Based Exams with a Two-Agent LLM Pipeline
Geoffrey Challen, Craig Zilles
Oral exams are compelling because (1) students can be asked to provide their reasoning for an answer and (2) their interactive nature permits follow-up questions to resolve ambiguous answers. But oral exams scale poorly. In this paper, we present scalable conversational assessment, an LLM-based system that conducts interactive text-based conversations with students to assess their ability to make and support an argument. We use a two-agent architecture to separate concerns and reduce the likelihood that answers are leaked to the student: the interviewer interacts directly with the student, but only receives guidance about the next question to ask the student; the hidden evaluator knows the goals of the whole activity, tracks the student's progress using a rubric, and guides the interviewer on when to follow-up on the current question or proceed to the next question. The system was first tested using a collection of simulated students with LLM personas of a particular ability level or adversarial tactic (e.g., answer-extractors, prompt-injectors, confident fabricators). A novel element of this evaluation was that it required the use of a fictional assessment topic to prevent personas that shouldn't have information from using knowledge present in the LLM's pre-training. The system was also deployed in a small, elective AI literacy course in both formative and summative contexts. Through manual and post-facto AI review of the transcripts we identified opportunities to improve the follow-up question generation and ensure that grading only credited ideas that the student (and not the interviewer) contributed.
